summary: Four-digit place value for ages 8-9: recognise the value of each digit in a four-digit number (in 7,345 the 7 is 7 thousands = 7000), partition and recompose (3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452), understand that thousands extend the same ×10 column pattern one place further, and handle multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050; 7,000) with correct placeholders and comma/space grouping. Building and recomposing numbers in a Th|H|T|O structure is the central activity for this objective; checking-style and reference activities support but are not a substitute for construction.
misconceptions: Mishandling multi-zero numbers (writing 'three thousand and six' as 3006 wrong-length, or 3,600).
Assigning the wrong value (the 7 in 7,345 read as 7 hundreds).
Concatenation of expanded parts (3000+400+50+2 written as 3000400502).
Misplacing or ignoring the thousands comma so magnitude is misread.

activities.title: Build and recompose in the Th|H|T|O bench
steps: Extend the familiar H|T|O column bench to Th|H|T|O and assemble a number such as 3,452 using thousand-cubes, hundred-flats, ten-rods and ones.
Drag ten hundred-flats into a tray and watch them fuse into one thousand-cube, saying aloud 'ten hundreds make one thousand' — the same unitising move one column up.
Keep three things in view at once as you build: the blocks, the numeral with its comma (3,452), and the expanded form 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2.
Use arrow (place-value) cards to lay out 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2, then slide them together so they overlap into the single numeral 3,452, linking the expanded form to the compact numeral.
Place the finished number on a 0-10,000 number line to check its rough magnitude, noticing how the comma/grouping helps you read size at a glance.

Swap two digits in your built number — for example exchange the 4 and the 5 in 3,452 to make 3,542 — and compare both on the bench and on the number line to see that moving a digit into a different column changes its value and the whole number's size.
Empty one column at a time (3,452 → 3,402 → 3,002) and describe what happens to the numeral and the expanded form.

In a reverse mode, listen to or read a spoken number such as 'three thousand and six' and build it; leave the hundreds AND tens columns empty so two bold placeholder 0s appear and the numeral resolves to 3,006 (not 36 or 3,600).
activities.insight: A digit's worth is set by its column, not by the digit itself — so swapping digits between columns changes the number; thousands repeat the ×10 pattern (ten hundreds = one thousand); and empty columns must still be written as 0 so magnitude and the comma are correct.

activities.title: Reference wall: one number decoded
steps: Study a single four-digit number displayed in a Th|H|T|O chart and tap each digit to reveal its blocks and its value (the 7 in 7,345 → 7 thousands = 7000).
Open a dedicated 3,006 anchor and use a flap or note that explains why the two internal zeros must both be written.
Use this wall as a lookup reference while working on other construction tasks.
activities.insight: Each digit's value can be read directly from its column, and internal zeros are placeholders that hold a column's place.

activities.title: Check digit values and expanded form
steps: Answer 'value of the digit' questions, e.g. state the value of the 7 in 7,345 (7000, not 7 or 700).
Complete fill-in-the-blank expanded forms: 3,452 = 3000 + ___ + 50 + 2 (blank is 400); 4,050 = 4000 + ___ + 50 + ___ (both blanks are 0).
Match numerals to their expanded forms and spoken number names.
For 'three thousand and six', identify the correct written form 3,006 and explain why the incorrect forms 36 and 3,600 must be rejected.
activities.insight: Learners can reliably read off a digit's value by its place and write/complete expanded forms, including where a column is zero.

activities.title: Spot the place-value detective's mistake
steps: Work with a character who keeps mis-sizing numbers such as 3,006 (writing 36 or 3,600).
Explain, using a column chart, why the character is wrong and correct the number together.
Say back the rule in your own words: empty hundreds and tens still need a 0 so the thousands digit keeps its place.
activities.insight: Articulating why a multi-zero number must be written a particular way deepens understanding of placeholders.

checkQuestion: In the number 3,452, what is the value of the 4? Would that value change if I wrote 3,542 instead? Why?
checkAnswer: In 3,452 the 4 is worth 4 hundreds (400). In 3,542 the same digit 4 is worth 4 tens (40). The value changes because the digit's place — not the digit itself — determines its worth.
